# Transcription of Handwritten Notes

---

## Column 1

### Process VM vs. System VM (written as "Sim VM")

| Process VM | System VM (Sim VM) |
| :--- | :--- |
| • Provide platform to create a single process or application | • Provide complete OS environment to run multiple applications |
| • Support one running process at a time | • Simulate entire hardware ($h/w$) |
| • Platform-independent program execution | • To run multiple OS instances on one host |
| • Guest OS not required | • Each VM has its own guest OS |
| • Java Virtual Machine (JVM), Parrot VM | • VMware, Citrix Xen |
| • Best for specific language-based apps | • May have slight overhead due to hardware ($h/w$) simulation |

---

### Emulation
*   Makes one system/simulator imitate another
*   Medium speed
*   **Example:** Use cross-platform software ($s/w$)

---

### Interpretation
*   Executes each instruction step-by-step
*   Slow
*   Used for debugging or testing

---

### Binary Translation
*   Converts entire instruction blocks
*   Two types:
    *   **Static translation:** Convert entire program before execution
    *   **Dynamic translation:** Convert during execution (used by VMware)
*   Fast
*   Used in VMware full virtualization

---

## Column 2

### Diagram: OS-Level Virtualization Architecture

```
+-----------------------------------+
|   [App]       [App]       [App]   |
|   VM 3        VM 2        VM 1    |
+-----------------------------------+
|           Common Kernel           |
+-----------------------------------+
|         Operating System          |
+-----------------------------------+
|             Hardware              |
+-----------------------------------+
```

#### Pedagogical Description of the Diagram:
The diagram illustrates the architecture of **OS-Level Virtualization** (also known as containerization). 
*   **Bottom Layer (Hardware):** Labeled as "$h/w$", representing the physical machine resources.
*   **Operating System Layer (OS):** The host operating system running directly on the hardware.
*   **Common Kernel Layer:** A shared kernel provided by the host OS that is utilized by all virtual environments.
*   **Top Layer (Virtual Machines / Containers):** Labeled as **VM1**, **VM2**, and **VM3**, each running its own application (**App**). Unlike traditional hardware virtualization, there is no hypervisor or separate guest OS for each VM; instead, they all share the single **Common Kernel** of the host OS.

---

### OS-Level Virtualization
*   Also called system-level or shared-kernel virtualization.
*   No hypervisor is used.
*   Instead, the kernel of the host OS itself creates and manages multiple virtual servers.

#### Key Points:
*   **No Host-Guest Paradigm:**
    *   Unlike machine virtualization, there is no distinct host OS and guest OS.
    *   Virtual Machines (VMs) in the traditional sense and hypervisors are not used.
*   **No Hypervisor:**
    *   The OS kernel directly manages all virtual environments.
*   **Shared Kernel:**
    *   All virtual servers share the same kernel as the host OS.
    *   Since they share the same kernel, all virtual servers (VS) must use the same OS type as the parent host.
*   **Purpose:**
    *   To create multiple Virtual Servers (VS) over a single OS kernel.
*   **Examples:**
    *   FreeBSD Jail
    *   Linux VServer
